description: The harp is described as Egyptian, Assyrian, Hebrew, Greek, Anglo-Saxon, and Irish, and existed during the time of Joseph, in early Christian times, and in early German times. A _rotta_ resembles a lyre held by a Hebrew from the time of Joseph. The bagpipe is described as Hebrew, Greek, and Celtic in origin. Bells are described as Hebrew and Peruvian, used for ringing, with Chinese bells and drums and flutes mentioned. The drum is described as Hebrew and Greek. The dulcimer is mentioned with Assyrian, Hebrew, and Persian prototypes. The Anglican cithara is noted. Al-Farabi performed on the lute. There are 59 references to the value of inquiry in the text. Arab instruments are described as numerous. The Ashantee trumpet is referenced.

The kinnor, a stringed instrument likely a lyre or small triangular harp, is considered the oldest Hebrew stringed instrument and is associated with King David, who is said to have suspended it over his pillow. It is linked to Jubal and resembles the kithara and kissar. The Hebrew lyre, simpler than other stringed instruments, preceded them in antiquity. Accounts by Josephus differ from biblical descriptions, possibly due to changes over time influenced by neighboring cultures. The kinnor is sometimes used generically for stringed instruments. The psalterion, possibly synonymous with the psanterin in Daniel, may have given rise to the santir, an oriental dulcimer. Saraswati, the Hindu goddess of music and speech, is depicted playing a lute-like stringed instrument while seated on a peacock. Eastern instruments, including the santir and kanoon, provide insight into ancient Egyptian and biblical musical traditions.

The juruparis is a sacred Indian instrument from the Rio Haupés, kept hidden in a forest stream where no one drinks or bathes; women and youths are restricted from seeing it, with women executed if they do. It is made with inner parts of the Paxiaba palm and blown during feasts outside houses of entertainment. A Caroados war trumpet closely resembles it, made of wood and producing a deep, pleasant sound, used by the chief to signal and sustain battle. A wooden trumpet found near the Orinoco by Gumilla also resembles the juruparis. Bottles filled with water, suspended from a curved tube, produce soothing sounds to lull drowsy chiefs during hot hours, with the sound fading due to evaporation. Various trumpets—Assyrian, Hebrew, Greek, Roman, American Indian, Caroados, and Mexican—are documented, with the conch used for war signals. Musical instruments in bas-reliefs resemble Chinese ones and are described by European travelers.

Sonorous stones, used by the Chinese as rhythmic instruments, include a single stone called tse-king and ten relics in Peking’s Confucius temple, shaped like drums and cut about three thousand years ago, bearing nearly obliterated primitive Chinese characters. The Chinese attributed high antiquity to the tchou, a percussion instrument made from kieou-mou wood with a stem resembling pine and foliage like cypress, featuring a central aperture for a wooden hammer handle secured by a pin that allows lateral movement when struck. The tchoung-tou, consisting of twelve bamboo slips banded at one end and expandable like a fan, was used for writing before paper was invented. Confucius, who lived about B.C. 500, expressed a desire to be a "wooden-tongued bell of heaven," a herald proclaiming divine purposes to the people, reflecting the symbolic use of such bells in military and ceremonial contexts. The Chinese also used wooden-tongued bells for calling people together when imperial messengers issued commands.

The cheng is a traditional Chinese wind instrument of high antiquity, consisting of 13, 19, or 24 tubes arranged in a calabash with a long curved mouthpiece; it was formerly known as yu and is associated with free reed construction. The free reed, originating in China in the cheng, was later adopted in European organ design, notably by Kratzenstein in St. Petersburg during the reign of Catharine II. Percussion instruments of definite sonorousness are chiefly found in China, Japan, Burma, Siam, and Java, contrasting with percussion instruments of indefinite sonorousness like drums and rattles, which are more universally known. Castanets, including crotala and crusmata, are types of percussion instruments. Some instruments in China originated in Hindustan and were diffused through East Asia to Japan. Ancient Chinese instruments may be studied in the Buddhist temple ruins of Ongcor-Wat and Ongcor-Thôm in Cambodia.

King David is depicted playing the *rotta*, a five-stringed instrument of oblong square shape resembling the Welsh *crwth*, in multiple manuscripts including an eighth-century one from the cathedral library of Durham and a seventh-century psalter (Cott. Vesp. A. I.) in the British Museum. The *rotta* is also shown in a tenth-century manuscript (Vitellius F. XI). David’s favorite instrument, the Hebrew *kinnor*, is rendered as a harp in English Bible translations due to the Greek term *kinyra*. In Anglo-Saxon manuscripts from the ninth and eleventh centuries in the British Museum, gleemen are shown playing the lyre and a double-pipe, the latter known as *mam* and frequently depicted. David is also shown holding hammers and striking bells suspended on a wooden stand. The *rotta* and other instruments reflect early musical traditions, with little improvement in European instrument construction over nearly a thousand years. The bagpipe has ancient origins in Ireland, mentioned in tenth-century Irish poetry and prose.

The Peruvians and Mexicans developed diverse musical traditions, including flutes, pipes, whistles, and drums. Peruvians used specific musical intervals for different songs, with each poem or song tied to a unique tune, conveying emotional states through instruments like the flute. They possessed a stringed instrument called *tinya*, resembling a guitar, and used agricultural songs with the word *hailli* ("Triumph") to glorify the Inca. Peruvian musical vessels mimicked animal cries and were used for amusement. The Mexicans used baked clay whistles, some grotesquely shaped and depicting humans, birds, beasts, and flowers, and employed flutes like the *cuyvi*, *huayllaca*, and *chayna*, the latter evoking sadness. Both cultures had flutes still used by Indian tribes; flutes from Palenque are in the Mexico museum. The Peruvians celebrated lugubrious songs during funerals, and their musical intervals were considered arbitrary rather than premeditated. Instruments like the whistle and flute are noted as prehistoric, with Mexican references.

The Hebrews attributed the origin of musical instruments to man, with Jubal identified in Genesis as the father of those who handle harps and organs, though he may have been seen as the first professional cultivator of instrumental music rather than the inventor. The Hebrews possessed thirty-six musical instruments during the time of David and Solomon, though only about half are mentioned in the Bible. Knowledge of their construction is limited, derived mainly from Egyptian and Assyrian instruments. Greek stringed instruments, such as the nabla, sambuka, barbiton, and magadis, are believed to have originated in Asia, with the magadis being uncertain as either stringed or wind and possibly resembling a dulcimer. The harp, depicted on a Greek vase from the time of Alexander the Great in the Munich museum, resembles the Assyrian harp and has thirteen strings, suggesting it was imported from Asia. Greek instruments appear to have Asiatic origins, and Egyptian influence on Greek music is considered overrated. The lyre is the only stringed instrument commonly depicted in Greek pottery, while the harp is less common but notable.

The botuto, a baked clay trumpet used by Indian tribes near the Orinoco River, ranges from three to four feet in length, with versions having two or three bellies; the two-belly variant produces a deep, terrifying sound and is used in mourning and funeral dances. Observed by Alexander von Humboldt, it is distinct from musical instruments in some classifications. Bone-flutes, about six inches long and with five finger-holes, have been found at Truxillo and are housed in the British Museum; one has a smaller hole and remnants of resinous substance in its aperture, which was used to narrow the end and facilitate sound production. A similar method is still used by some Indian tribes in Guiana to construct bone-flutes. A pottery instrument with four finger-holes produces four sounds when three are open, with the fourth hole lowering pitch by a semitone. Indian tribes today have lower musical abilities than their ancestors, and several of their instruments are considered primitive and not worthy of classification as musical instruments. A copper bell from an ancient Peruvian tomb is in the museum at Lima.

Music played central roles in religious and royal ceremonies across ancient cultures. In Assyria, a group of eleven instrumental performers and a chorus of female and child singers performed, with one female singer mimicking Persian traditions. Monarchs, including Darius, used musical metaphors in prayers, with the new ruler likened to a flute that must be "breathed into" to receive divine guidance. The Inca offered thanksgiving at the Temple of the Sun after battle victories, followed by music and dancing. Nezahualcoyotl built a temple dedicated to "the unknown god, the cause of causes," with musical instruments on a nine-story tower to summon worshippers. In Jerusalem, David and Solomon maintained royal bands for sacred music. A tradition in Swedish and Scotch ballads tells of a harper who built his instrument from the bones and golden hair of a girl drowned by a wicked woman, and her music killed the murderer. In Peru, priests and minstrels composed sacred music, and musical performances were used to convert indigenous populations. King Darius, during his fasting, excluded music, indicating its regular presence in court life.

The lyre, a stringed instrument held horizontally, has strings tied to a front bar that can be adjusted to change pitch: pushing upwards increases tension and raises pitch, while pushing downwards lowers it. Its strings are commonly made of catgut (from sheep, goat, camel, etc.) or sinew, and can be played with fingers or a plectrum, such as the short ivory or metal plektron. Stringed instruments without a fingerboard, including the dulcimer, are played by twanging with fingers, wood, horn, metal, or a plectrum. The _ou_, an ancient Chinese percussion instrument made of wood with metal pieces resembling saw teeth, is struck with a plectrum or _tchen_. Musical instruments are commonly constructed from wood, metal, and animal hide, with tropical regions using bamboo, cane, and gourds. The carillon uses metal rods for manual keys and wooden pedal keys, requiring dexterity and physical power. Popular songs, originating from the heart, possess natural expression, health, and vigour, contrasting with artificial compositions that arise from fingers or pen and lack these qualities.

The tambourine, either round or oblong with incurved sides, is used in Europe and the East. Parchment, used in drums like the *huehuetl* and the Egyptian drum, was stretched over wooden cylinders and tightened with cords; the *huehuetl* was covered at the top with deer-skin and struck with fingers. The *po-fou*, a drum about one foot four inches long and seven inches in diameter, had parchment at each end, boiled in water, and was sometimes filled with rice husk to mellow its sound. The *tympanum*, resembling the tambourine and beaten with hands, was covered with parchment on both sides. A tympanum in the triple portal of the Portico della Gloria, executed in 1188, contains twenty-four seated figures from the Apocalypse, each holding a musical instrument. The Egyptian drum, two to three feet long, was braced by cords and carried on a shoulder band. The *doff*, *diff*, and *adufe* are small hand-drums synonymous with the Hebrew *toph*.

The rotta, a medieval stringed instrument played by twanging or bow, is referred to as cithara teutonica and may have originated from Celtic races in the British Isles, with its name possibly evolving from chrotta. It had up to twenty strings and is linked to the Irish cionar cruit and the Welsh crwth, which had few strings and a finger-board. The bow was first applied to instruments like the cithara or psalterium. Hindus use the suroda as both a lute and fiddle and claim to have invented the violin bow, asserting that the ravanastron—an ancient bow-played instrument invented by Ravanon, a king of Ceylon—dates back five thousand years. The ravanastron is found among lower classes in mountainous areas and resembles Arabian and Persian instruments, typically used by higher classes in towns. The Anglo-Saxon fiddle (fithele) is pear-shaped with four strings and no bridge, while the violin is played with pizzicato. The origin of the violin bow is debated, with Hindus claiming invention, and the lyre possibly being a prototype of the violin bow.

The _magrepha_, described in the Talmud as a powerful organ in Jerusalem’s temple, consists of a wind-chest with ten pipes, each capable of emitting ten different sounds via finger-holes, allowing for one hundred distinct sounds, and includes two pairs of bellows and ten keys played with fingers; its tone was extremely loud and could be heard at great distances. Authorities debate whether it was an organ, bagpipe, or kettle-drum, with a syrinx with bellows from ancient Tarsus possibly indicating the Hebrew bagpipe’s form. The _magrepha_ is not mentioned in the Bible. An illustration from the twelfth century in Eadwine’s psalter at Trinity College, Cambridge, shows an early organ with ten to fourteen pipes, some double, requiring six men—four for wind and two to play and manage supply. The regal, a percussion instrument resembling a harmonica, was known in 18th-century England and described by Grassineau as sticks bound with beads struck to produce harmony. A Hebrew lyre, possibly from the time of Joseph, is depicted in an ancient Egyptian painting at Beni Hassan.

The Indians of Mexico crafted the acocotl, a thin tube 8–10 feet long, not thicker than a couple of inches, made from the dry stalk of a plant, which they also called acocotl. It is played by inhaling through a mouthpiece resembling a clarinet, requiring strong lungs, and is now more commonly known as the clarin, a name given by Spaniards. The instrument ends in a bell and has a small mouthpiece. In Chile, the Araucanians made flutes from enemy or animal bones, especially from prisoners, using them to play mournful war-songs during dances, with flutes from enemy bones reserved for warriors. A similar instrument, described by S. S. Hill, consists of two earthen vessels shaped like india-rubber bottles connected by a flat tube with a small hole. The teponaztli, a drum, varied in size, some over five feet long and audible up to three miles, and was carried on a string or worn on the neck. These instruments and musical practices reflect ancient traditions, some preserved in remote tribes, though three centuries of oppression suppressed melodic expressions once common among indigenous peoples.

The huayra-puhura is a wind instrument used by American Indians, made of cane and greenish talc, with some versions containing eight pipes and others fourteen reed pipes arranged in two rows. One variant has lateral finger-holes on the second, fourth, sixth, and seventh pipes, which lower the pitch a semitone when closed; other pipes produce unalterable tones. The instrument produces tones according to the pentatonic scale, with evidence of intentional design, though the highest octave is indistinct due to damage. It is associated with the word "huayra," meaning "air," and was sometimes ornamented with embroidery featuring twelve figures resembling Maltese crosses, suggesting a cross design used by American Indians in art and sculpture. Several specimens found in tombs and hiding places are genuine pre-Columbian inventions, revealing characteristics of the indigenous musical system. Variations in intervals—thirds, fourths, fifths, sixths, and octaves—were observed across specimens, though the pentatonic scale is consistently present. The instrument is linked to Peruvian traditions and is noted in museum collections, including the British Museum and a French collection.

The sackbut, a metal instrument resembling an early trombone, was known in the ninth century and is associated with the English term possibly derived from sambuca; it is illustrated in a woodcut and linked to the French terms sacqueboute and saquebutte. The vielle, a French instrument from about 1550 bearing Henry II monograms, is housed at South Kensington. The recorder, mentioned in Hamlet’s stage direction and illustrated in a 1683 London publication, is now rare. The lute, originating in China, Persia, and Moorish regions, evolved from four strings to twelve by the sixteenth century, with eleven strings (five pairs and one single chanterelle) being most common; it was as popular as the pianoforte in the Elizabethan era. The virginal is illustrated in an Elizabethan engraving at South Kensington. South Kensington holds notable instrument collections, especially those with elegant shapes and Asiatic ornamentation, including a cast of Exeter Cathedral’s minstrels’ gallery. The recorder and lute are among the instruments described in the book *Musical Instruments* by Carl Engel, published in London.

The crwth, particularly the three-stringed crwth trithant, was used by the inferior class of Welsh bards and is described as a rebeck, similar to the Moorish fiddle favored by itinerant Breton bards who call it rébek. A bas-relief from Worcester Cathedral, dating to the twelfth or thirteenth century, depicts a crowned player on the crwth. In an eleventh-century illumination from the Bibliothèque royale, musicians with uncovered heads play psalteriums alongside the player. The psalterium, a triangular or square stringed instrument, was designated in Latin medieval texts and had a trapezium shape akin to the dulcimer; a small psalterium with a sound-board is the prototype of the citole, a finger-played dulcimer. The nablum, from a ninth-century manuscript at Angers, shares acoustic qualities with the cithara, which is described as an improvement over the triangular psalterium due to its small sound-board. Medieval writers used vague, changing names for instruments, and musicians generally did not focus on instrument-national style connections. A player, often the church organist and carilloneur, wears leathern gloves to protect fingers during performance.

The chanterelle, a high-pitched English lute, had 24 strings arranged in 12 pairs—six over the finger-board and six on the side—and was more properly classified as a theorbo. Both the lute and theorbo featured frets made of catgut, fastened at proper distances to ensure chromatic succession, with fret positions marked by letters (a, b, c, etc.) in lute music notation. The theorbo, popular in the sixteenth century, had strings on the finger-board and additional bass strings on its left side, with the archlute and chitarrone being its largest forms. The organistrum, a musical instrument with keys on the neck raised by handles, required two performers—one to turn the wheel and one to operate the keys—and is considered a predecessor of the hurdy-gurdy. A musician’s instrument was smaller than the smallest viola da gamba, and viol players typically carried a chest of six viols (two basses, two tenors, two trebles). The tumbler in a group of crowned minstrels is likely the vocalist, as he has no instrument.

Stringed instruments vary in form, power of sound, and compass and include Greek, Roman, and Peruvian types; they are a category of musical instruments and include ancient forms like kin and chê, which are dulcimers still in use and housed in the South Kensington Museum. A ninth-century manuscript from the St. Blasius monastery in the Black Forest, which contained illustrations of a cithara, was destroyed by fire in 1768, but abbot Gerbert preserved tracings of its illustrations and published them in 1774 in *De cantu et musica sacra*. These illustrations were derived from the manuscript. Clavigero claims the Mexicans were unacquainted with stringed instruments, a claim challenged by their high level of civilization. Stringed instruments are generally found in nations with inferior intellectual progress, and foreign instruments in the South Kensington collection show that the traditional classification into stringed, wind, and percussion instruments is invalid globally. Traditions attribute the invention of stringed instruments to Fohi (c. B.C. 3000) and Niuva, who lived at his time. All such instruments lack a fore pillar.

The Arabs adopted Persian musical systems and instruments after conquering Persia in A.D. 641, with early Arab music theory based on Persian precedent, dividing the octave into seventeen one-third-tones still used in the East. Instruments like the lute and tamboura have frets calibrated for these intervals. Al-Farabi, a 10th-century theorist, does not mention the fiddle-bow, supporting theories of its origin in England or Wales, though Sanskrit scholars indicate it existed in Hindustan as early as 1500–2000 years ago. The rebab and kemangeh, both Persian in origin, were adopted by Arabs and used in Spain, where Moorish instruments spread to France, Germany, and England. Ash-shakandi, living in Spain around A.D. 1200, references the rebab, which was considered rudimentary. Persian instruments like the chang (a harp-like instrument) and tschenk (a dulcimer-like instrument) are known, with the chang possibly linked to Turkish music derived from Persia. A 1203 event in Ossemer records a lightning strike killing 24 people while a parson played a fiddle, highlighting the fiddle-bow’s presence in Europe. Stringed instruments played with a bow are known across Asia, Africa, and Europe, with Persian and Arab instruments showing clear eastern roots.

The lyre, depicted in an engraving alongside a lyre-player, another man, and strange animals, differs from Egyptian lyres and is found in the British Museum in forms with three, five, or six strings; its frame may be made of animal horn or wood shaped to imitate horns. The cornu, a large bronze curved horn, is held under the arm with the broad end upwards over the shoulder and is shown in the engraving with the tuba and lituus, both used in war for signaling. Wind instruments of flute and trumpet kinds are widespread and often made from animal horns, bones, tusks, vegetable substances, or metal. The sistrum consists of a bronze or brass frame with three or four metal bars that produce a jingling noise when shaken. The shophar, a curved horn made of ram’s horn, is still used in Jewish religious services and is mentioned in the Bible; the kantele, a Finnish harp without a front pillar, was used until the present century. The bagpipe, made from goat skin and retaining the animal’s shape including horns, is known as *kosa* and was favored by Nero. The Amazon-stone produces a metallic sound when struck by a hard substance and was cut into thin plates by American Indians for use as a musical instrument.

The mishrokitha, mentioned in Daniel, is likely a product of artistic imagination and depicted as a small organ with seven pipes and a mouthpiece, showing European characteristics in its design. A bas-relief from the end of the eleventh century, originally from St. Georges de Boscherville and now in the Museum of Rouen, shows twelve performers, most wearing crowns, including a first performer playing a viol held between the knees, slightly larger than the smallest viola da gamba. The viol, which existed in various forms with differing string tunings and sizes, may have originated earlier than previously thought due to its two playing positions. Machalath, gittith, and nechiloth are generally considered musical instruments—machalath and gittith as stringed instruments, nechiloth as a flute—mentioned in Psalms. The trigonon species features an instrument held horizontally and twanged with a bent plectrum, frequently shown in groups of two or more on bas-reliefs. In 1661, John Elliot translated the Psalms into Indian verse, with Indian converts singing metrical psalms described as excellent and most ravishing, surpassing European sacred vocal performances. Most ancient nations attributed musical instrument invention to gods or superhuman beings.

The syrinx, a Pandean pipe with three to nine tubes (usually seven), is depicted in eleventh-century illustrations with tubes inserted into a bowl-shaped box, possibly representing the *frestele*, *fretel*, or *fretiau*. It is one of the instruments in the sculpture at South Kensington, which includes the cittern, bagpipe, clarion, rebec, psaltery, sackbut, regals, gittern, shalm, timbrel, and cymbals. The vihuela resembles the rebec and has three strings, with one or two instances indicating five tuning-pegs; a larger vihuela has a broader body, incurvations at the sides, and different sound-holes. Bamboo is used to make flutes (ty, yo, tché), the koan-tsee (12 tubes), and the siao (16 tubes), while the pai-siao differs by having its tubes inserted into an oddly-shaped, ornamented case with grotesque designs and silken appendages. The turé, a loud and harsh bamboo trumpet used by Amazonian Indian tribes in war, resembles Hindu trumpets (tooree or tootooree) and is used by sentinels on lofty trees to signal attacks.

The Assyrian harp, about four feet high and lacking a front pillar, was depicted in bas-reliefs from Nimrud, Khorsabad, and Kouyunjik near the Tigris River in Asiatic Turkey; it had sound-holes shaped like an hour-glass and tuning-pegs in regular order, with strings possibly made of silk or catgut. Ancient Egyptians used catgut on harps and had musical instruments accurately depicted in sculptures and paintings, which are more reliable than frescoes due to less restoration. The Persian *chang*, a harp with a triangular frame, resembled the Assyrian harp in construction and size, and was a favorite instrument before falling into disuse. Sculptures at Tackt-i-Bostan near Kermanshah, created during Khosroo Purviz’s lifetime, depict a woman playing a *trigonon*, a triangular instrument with a third bar added for strength, and show religious observances beginning at sunrise, mid-day, sunset, and midnight. Both Assyrians and Babylonians used instrumental music in religious observances, as confirmed by Nebuchadnezzar’s command to worship a golden image when hearing music including harp, flute, and psaltery. Restorers may have made slight brush touches at sound-holes, screws, or curvatures, altering appearances and impairing evidence value for musical investigators.

The *nofre*, a guitar-like instrument nearly identical to the modern tamboura, was a favorite among ancient Egyptians, appearing in hieroglyphs as a symbol of 'good' and in concert representations dating before B.C. 1500. It demonstrates early Egyptian mastery of music through its finger-board, enabling more notes on few strings, surpassing harps in note production. The *nofre* is found in well-preserved frescoes at Thebes, including a fragment in the British Museum showing two women playing it with visible frets. Bruce discovered elegant harps in frescoes at Thebes, believed to be from Rameses III’s tomb, which created a sensation among musicians due to their form and decoration, though some doubted their authenticity. A triangular harp of Egyptian origin with 21 strings is in the Louvre. A sculptured cross at Ullard, dated before 800 and older than Monasterboice, features rudimentary harp-like figures with uncertain string count. In Spain, the 12th-century sculpture 'John in the Apocalypse' depicts musicians with instruments representative of the period, including a central organistrum, small harps (identical to Anglo-Saxon harps), triangular harps, and a salterio resembling a dulcimer. A *pito*, a flute-like instrument, has been found in well-preserved condition with a pentatonic scale, and a variant is housed in the British Museum. At a festival honoring Tezcatlepoca, a young man was sacrificed after being taught to play the flute.

Ringers manage two bells each, and with seven ringers, fourteen different tones are produced. Each ringer can substitute two other bells to enable complex compositions with modulations, requiring good timeists and precise timing. Musical instruments from foreign nations yield valuable hints for improving or inventing new instruments, and such inventions often lead to the adoption of new musical effects in compositions. Musical instruments reveal characteristic features of a nation’s musical compositions, including intervals, scales, and modulations. These features are central to understanding the structure and style of musical compositions.

The monochord, featuring a single string stretched over two bridges on an oblong box and adjustable via a turning screw, was primarily used by theorists for teaching singing and acoustics, not musical performance. Its intervals, marked on the side and regulated by a movable bridge, followed a diatonic scale with a chromatic seventh interval including both b-flat and b-natural, as noted in tenth-century notation. The octave is produced in pipes when closed at one end, with stopped diapason pipes being half the length of open ones but producing the same pitch with a less bright sound. In ancient China, bells known as tchung, including the square té-tchung (also called piao), made of copper alloyed with tin in a 1:6 ratio, were used to indicate time and musical divisions. The pien-king and other Chinese instruments are tuned to twelve lu intervals per octave, while the soung-king is four intervals lower than the pien-king. The Hindus divided their scale into twenty-two sruti intervals, smaller than modern semitones, within an octave.

The vina is a Hindu instrument and the principal national instrument of Hindustan, invented by the god Nareda and also known as cach’-hapi, meaning tortoise, with testudo being an alternative name for tortoise. It has seven wire strings, movable frets fastened with wax that allow the performer to regulate the scale or mode, and two hollowed gourds attached to increase its sonorousness. The vina exists in various forms across different districts of Hindustan, with many instruments known by different names and varieties. A celebrated virtuoso on the vina, Jeewan Shah, lived about a hundred years ago. Most instruments popular about a hundred years ago are now either disused or significantly altered, considered almost new inventions. The vina is listed among Hindu instruments from pages 46 to 48.

The hiuen-tchung was an antique Chinese musical instrument with an oval shape and a crescent-shaped mouth, featuring ornamentation similar to the té-tchung, which included symbolical figures arranged in four divisions, each containing nine mammals. These figures had deep meanings related to the seasons and Buddhist religion. The hiuen-tchung was present among the instruments at the time of Confucius and became widely used during the Han dynasty (200 B.C.–200 A.D.). The largest hiuen-tchung was about twenty inches long and was sounded with a wooden mallet having an oval knob, similar to the té-tchung. The ur-heen, a two-stringed instrument with a wooden body covered in serpent skin, is almost identical to the ravanastron and was introduced into China after the introduction of Buddhism; it was not previously mentioned in Chinese instruments.

The cymbalum is a musical instrument made of two metal plates, similar to modern cymbals, which can be clashed or constructed with bells; it produces shrill sounds and is illustrated in woodcuts. The bunibulum consists of an angular frame with loosely attached metal plates, producing noise by shaking and resembling the sistrum; it is also illustrated in woodcuts. The triangle is a musical instrument resembling the triangle in use today, with metal ornamentation in the middle, and is occasionally used in the orchestra. The Romans had a triangulum similar to the modern triangle. The orchestra underwent significant modification in scarcely more than a century. Woodcuts illustrate the cymbalum, bunibulum, and triangle. Relics help reveal manners and customs and assist in understanding forefathers. Metal plates were similar to cymbals.

The shalm, or shawm, is a musical instrument with a reed in its mouth-hole and is considered a poor ancestor of the modern oboe and clarinet; it is similar in construction to the wait, an English wind instrument with a reed and mouth-hole, differing only in size, and was used by watchmen to proclaim the time of night. The wait is also a musical instrument and is linked to watchmen and timekeeping. The tibia is a musical instrument originally made from shin bone, featuring a mouth-hole and four finger-holes, later constructed from other materials while retaining its shape. The tibia gingrina consists of a long thin reed tube with a mouth-hole at the side of one end. Both shalm and tibia are classified as musical instruments. A Roman girl and tibia are listed as musical instruments.

In Greece, particularly on Zante and other islands, church bells are housed in separate belfries to prevent damage during earthquakes, as falling bells could destroy the roof and lead to complete building destruction. Etruscan tombs contain numerous bronze bells of varying sizes and tones, indicating an ancient cultural use of bells. Church bells are suspended to allow effective vibration without damaging the building, with methods differing by region—such as timber frameworks in Servia or oak trees in Russia. The roof of Peterborough Cathedral, built between 1177 and 1194, was repaired in 1835, casting doubt on early depictions of violin-like instruments. In Greece, several instruments used by musicians who immigrated from Asia are not considered national instruments. Bells are also used for signaling, as seen in England and Mexico, and carillons lack vibration-stopping mechanisms, causing confusion when heard closely but clarity at a distance.

The Egyptians used various musical instruments, including trumpets, three kinds of tambourines or hand drums, three kinds of barrel-shaped drums, gongs, bells, cymbals, and castanets. They used straight drumsticks with a handle and knob, some of which are in the Berlin Museum. North American Indians were noted by old writers for their innate musical talent and were converted to Christianity after the Puritans settled in New England. Their musical instruments, including drums of odd shapes like sugar-loaf, flutes, and whistles, are displayed in the Kenningham Museum, described in its large catalogue. Some of these items, such as rattles, drums, flutes, and whistles, are specifically attributed to North American Indians. In western Africa, some <DW64>s affixed human skulls to their drums.

Nareda, meaning "the giver of water," is a water spirit and ruler of the clouds, similar to Nereus and his musical Nereides. In Sanskrit tradition, "nara" means water, and Nareda embodies the divine origin of water. Musical water-spirits originated as rain deities, with music derived from clouds, supporting the heavenly origin of music. The chelys, a small lyre made of tortoise shell or imitation wood, was crafted by Hermes and associated with water-based musical traditions. Odin, known as the originator of magic songs and ruler of the sea, is called Nikarr and played a harp in the sea's depth, teaching humans through subordinate spirits. Beliefs that music originated from water stem from a common pre-historic source, possibly linked to the Aryan race’s spread, and are preserved in Icelandic national songs, the Faroe Islands, Norway, and Denmark. The rhythmic flow of waves and running water inspired various nations to believe their instruments originated from water.

The flageolet is a wind instrument resembling the Aztec pito, a reddish pottery pipe with four finger-holes and a consistent pitch across specimens ranging from six to nine inches in length. The pito is similar in form to the flageolet, and a bronze flageolet-like flute was found in an Etruscan tomb. The sêbi, a single flute, requires the performer to extend their arms fully to reach its finger-hole and is also named after the leg-bone, suggesting it was originally made of bone. The Greeks used the term aulos for flutes and oboes, including flageolets and flûte à bec; the single flute was called monaulos. A finger-hole can alter pitch when closed, enabling different tones, while a ball of baked clay in some whistles vibrates to produce a shrill, whirring sound. Middle ages flutes were blown at the end like the flageolet. The sêbi is a musical instrument.

The Tezcucans (Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Aztecs but surpassed them in knowledge, social refinement, and advancement in the arts and sciences. Prescott observed that Tezcucan culture produced the best histories, poems, laws, and dialects, and that the Aztecs matched their neighbors in the splendor of their living and magnificence of structures, displaying a pomp and ostentatious pageantry considered truly Asiatic. The Aztecs held the flute and pipe in high esteem, using them in religious observances and solemn orations. They depicted yotl-bells in picture-writings as tribute objects, and these bells resemble Schellen affixed to German horses, used in winter for noiseless sledge drives. The Hebrew word *toph* is rendered as *timbrel* or *tabret*, a musical instrument used in processions and by females, and is similar to a tambourine or Egyptian darabouka. The British Museum holds a collection of Mexican antiquities including yotl-bells and timbrels.

The Greeks developed various lyres, including lyra, ithara, chelys, and phorminx, with the phorminx used for accompanying recitations and resembling the kithara. The kithara, with a square base held against the breast, was employed for solo performances as early as 700 B.C. and was adopted by the Greeks from the Lydians. The Romans adopted many Greek and Asian instruments, with the lyre—especially in forms like lyra, cithara, and chelys—being their favorite stringed instrument; they did not essentially improve these instruments, deriving some from the Etruscans who possessed instruments similar to the Greeks. The lyra, in general, referred to lyres with an oval base, and a German fiddle from the ninth century, copied from the manuscript of St. Blasius, had one string. The manuscript of St. Blasius also illustrates a harp with twelve strings and two sound holes. Through the Greeks and Romans, musical instruments were first well-authenticatedly introduced into Europe from Asia.

England has a distinct musical heritage, with old instruments such as those used during Queen Elizabeth’s time frequently mentioned in historical literature and requiring knowledge of shape and construction for understanding. Peal-ringing, a national pastime, dates back to 960 when Abbot Egelric of Croyland cast six bells, and typically involves eight bells attuned to the diatonic scale, sometimes extending to ten or twelve. The people of England were fond of loud noises like cannon firing, drums, and bell ringing, with London having a practice of individuals climbing belfries to ring bells for hours. Old instruments, including those in the violin class like the lute, possessed a high degree of variety in sound quality (clang-tint), which composers believe is more expressive than the uniformity of modern instruments. Modern instruments, though improved, lack variety in timbre, and earlier instruments were considered more beautiful. A war-trumpet from the King of Ashantee, brought to England and surrounded by human jawbones, highlights the cultural significance of musical instruments. National music exhibits distinctive characteristics that provide insight into human feelings and affinities, benefiting composers and performers.

The hydraulic organ, attributed by some to the Etruscans and known about 200 years before the Christian era, is more accurately a pneumatic organ, as sound was produced by a current of air through pipes, with water used to pressurize and regulate the bellows. Pipes were controlled by stops resembling modern organ stops. The device was compact, carried by one or two people and placed on a table. A coin of Emperor Nero shows the highest known example, featuring ten pipes and no keyboard. It was occasionally used in churches but more commonly in secular entertainments, such as circus or amphitheatre events, where victors received medals with impressions of the instrument. The hydraulic organ was entirely replaced by the pneumatic organ at the beginning of the fourteenth century. A pneumatic organ is sculpted on an obelisk erected in Constantinople under Theodosius the Great towards the end of the fourth century.

A small bone, identified as the first digital phalanx of a ruminant, was found in Dordogne, France, and is believed to have been used as a whistle in hunting, producing a shrill sound when blown into the lower lip. Three of its phalanges are from reindeer, one from chamois. A similar bone from the cave of Lombrive, in Ariège, also has drilled holes, and dog eye-teeth from the same site produce similar sounds. The poongi, a Hindu instrument resembling a bagpipe, consists of a gourd or Cuddos nut with two pipes and is played by snake charmers; it is also known as toumrie or magoudi, with the latter suggesting a link to ancient Greek bagpipes. The chorus, a wind instrument with one or two tubes, had versions resembling a bagpipe or the poongi and was also used for stringed instruments. Pipes and flutes, made of bone or pottery, are common in Aztec and Peruvian cultures and are preserved in original condition. Pottery and bone are durable materials used widely in musical instruments, including the ajacaxtli, a rattle made of pottery with pebbles inside. Human ingenuity has utilized horn, bone, glass, pottery, stone, and vibrating matter for music.

The museum at Kensington contains specimens of antique instruments from the last three centuries, including cither, virginal, spinet, clavichord, and harpsichord, which are valued by our forefathers. These instruments, such as viols, spinets, and old lutes, are elegant in shape and often ornamented with carvings, marquetry, and painting. A painting by Melozzo da Forli from the fifteenth century depicts a regal with keys resembling the pistons of brass instruments, suggesting historical connections between keyboard instruments and brass. The study of music, like scientific pursuits, requires tools; the unassisted eye sees only faint details, but with tools like a telescope, clearer insights emerge. An essay on music history helps clarify misty facts about musical instruments, and hints from instrument comparisons—such as between American Indian and eastern hemisphere instruments—may interest the reader. Improvements in brass instrument construction and new inventions during the present century have influenced modern orchestral works.

The pianoforte, invented in the beginning of the eighteenth century, evolved from the clavicembalo, which featured a keyboard and retained primitive dulcimer traits such as a trapezium shape and a round hole in the soundboard. The dulcimer, known as santir to the Arabs and Persians and as cimbal to Europeans, originated as a wooden board with few strings and influenced early keyboard instruments. The pianoforte's tones conform to the pentatonic scale, discernible by omitting f and b from the C major scale or striking black keys from f-sharp to f-sharp. A pedal, generally attributed to Bernard, a German living in Venice about 1470, was believed to have been invented earlier, and his practicable construction made it widely known. The carillon at Berlin’s Parochial-Kirche includes 37 bells and features both a keyboard and a pedal, offering over three octaves. In Western Europe, instruments of the harmonium class have become popular and nearly compete with the pianoforte. The Romans spread musical instruments to Western Europe through conquest.

The sistrum, denoted in 2 Samuel vi. 5 and translated as cymbals in the English Bible, is believed by Winer, Saalfchütz, and other commentators to be the instrument referred to as menaaneim. Cymbals, described as cymbalum and mentioned at page 113, are a type of metallic percussion instrument, including tzeltzclim, metziloth, and metzilthaim. Small golden bells, known as phaamon, were attached to the high-priest's robes and are also fastened today to the rolls of the Law, which are kept in synagogues. These golden bells are considered an ornamentation believed to have been in use from time immemorial. The sistrum is referred to as cymbals in the Bible, and cymbals are associated with the high-priest's vestments and sacred rituals.

The Council of Music in Tezcuco, founded by monarch Nezahualcoyotl, functioned as an academy for general education and is considered strong evidence of the intellectual attainments of the Mexican Indians before the discovery of America. It aimed to advance various arts, history, and astronomy and resembled the Chinese Board of Music (Yo Poo), which is connected to the Lé Poo established by the imperial government in Peking. Some inquirers believe the sonorous metal in Tezcuco’s great temple was a gong, claiming this based on detecting traces of a Mongol invasion about six hundred years ago; however, this theory is disputed, as a little Peruvian bell engraved on page 75 resembles a Buddhist hand-bell and provides more tangible evidence. The sonorous metal was struck with a mallet and may have been either a gong or a bell. Most musical instruments found among present-day American Indians are genuine old Indian contrivances that existed long before the discovery of America.

A flute-concert painted on a tomb in the pyramids of Gizeh, dating from before B.C. 2000, depicts eight musicians performing on flutes, with one standing musician clothed and possibly serving as the director or solo performer. Al-Farabi, a celebrated musician, traveled to the court of the caliph of Baghdad, disguised to avoid being retained in Asia, where he feared he would never see his home. At court, he performed on the lute, beginning in a musical mode that caused the audience to laugh, switching to another that induced sighing and sadness, and later to a mode that provoked rage, which he calmed by switching to an appeasing mode. He concluded with a mode that induced profound sleep in the audience. The caliph desired to hear Al-Farabi and sent messengers to Spain to bring him, offering rich presents. Al-Farabi, like the flutist Timotheus, used changing musical modes to arouse and subdue different emotions during his performance.

Historians often lack clarity in discussing musical aspects of indigenous cultures, as seen in J. Ranking’s unverified account of Montezuma’s repasts involving fiddle, flute, snail-shell, kettle-drum, and strange instruments, without citing a source. Some historians propose American Indians emigrated from Mongolia, Tibet, or Hindustan or are descendants of Phoenician colonists who settled in central America. The Board of Rites regulates ceremonies including sacrifices, festivals, marriages, deaths, and burials. In central America, Dominicans composed a sacred poem in the Guatemalan dialect narrating key biblical events, which they sang to natives with musical instruments. Musical performances were essential in Peruvian and central American public celebrations, and ancient instruments like the *teponaztli* resemble drums from Tonga, Fiji, and Torres Strait. Whistles and pipes from Chiriqui’s graves show about half a dozen tones; such instruments, made from fragile materials, are not preserved in museums. The African marimba has become popular among Guatemalan natives. Musical performances are considered key to understanding indigenous instruments.

A pipe made from stag’s-horn was found in a burying-place near Poitiers, France, dating from the latest time of the stone age. It has three equidistant finger-holes, is blown at the end like a flûte à bec, and produces four distinct tones, including the lowest when all holes are covered. Stone utensils and weapons were found with it, and two straws, along with thick straw pieces inserted into the tube, served as a reed-like component. The aulos, a variety of flute, differs from Egyptian flutes and pipes by being held like a flageolet and featuring a vibrating reed inserted into the mouth-piece, resembling an oboe or clarionet. Egyptian pipes are made of reed and have three to five or more finger-holes. Pipe types include single, double, Mexican, and Peruvian pipes; Peruvian pipes are a type of musical instrument used in Peru. The chayna has a reed like the oboe, and Hindustan has a type of oboe called shehna.

The tibia, a double flute instrument used by Romans, consisted of two tubes sharing or having separate mouth-pieces; when identical, it was called tibia pares, when different, tibia impares. Finger-holes regulated intervals, with small plugs inserted; tibia dextra came from the upper, thinner part of a reed, and tibia sinistra from the lower, broader part. Performers used the capistrum, a cheek band similar to the Greek phorbeia. A mosaic of a Roman girl playing the tibia, found in 1823 on the Via Appia, is in the British Museum and shows the holmos, a mouth-piece resembling an oboe reed. The diaulos, a cedar wood instrument from Athens with fifteen-inch tubes and one mouth-piece per tube, has six finger-holes—five on the upper side and one underneath—and is housed in the British Museum. The hiuen, a baked clay wind instrument from China, has five finger-holes (three on one side, two on the opposite) and produces tones in conformity with the pentatonic scale.

The sistrum, an Egyptian instrument with the name seshesh, was derived from Egypt and introduced with the worship of Isis; its bars are often shaped like snakes or end in a goose head, sometimes featuring metal rings, and its frame may include a cat figure. It was primarily used by females in religious ceremonies and measures between nine and eighteen inches in length, with the largest at 18 inches. The sistrum is also known as a Hebrew and Roman musical instrument. Egyptian cymbals, resembling modern cymbals, are housed in the British Museum and were found in a coffin containing a sacred musician’s mummy, displayed alongside it. A Greek lyre fragment, found near Athens, has a wooden frame about 18 inches long with a 9-inch cross-bar and is also housed in the British Museum. Bronze bells, held in the British Museum, range from 0.75 to 2.25 inches in height and have a hole near the top for a clapper, though none of the bells in this type had a clapper. Roman musical instruments include the lyre.

The *king* is a sacred Chinese musical instrument, 2200 years old, used to accompany songs of praise and played before the emperor at early morning during religious observances, when incense was burned. It was constructed from different species of stones, primarily *yu*, which is sonorous, beautiful, hard, heavy, and found in mountain streams and rock crevices; large specimens up to three feet in diameter are rare. *Yu* retains a constant pitch regardless of temperature, humidity, or dryness and is valued for its stability. The Chinese preferred certain colors for the *king* across centuries. Stones were carved into grotesque shapes, including bats with outstretched wings, fishes, and ancient Chinese bells. The *pien-tchung*, a set of sixteen bells, shares the same musical scale as the *king*. One of its vibrating tongues is thinner than the other, with pitch regulated by shaving wood. Uncivilized nations view bright, glittering, and rare items as ornamental. A Congolese instrument, decorated with a broken looking-glass fragment and brass buttons bearing Louis XVI, was observed by Captain Tuckey, possibly linked to a drowned French sailor. European mineralogists considered *yu* a type of agate.
